name: AppSelectBench: Application-Level Tool Selection Benchmark
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2511.19957 [cs.CL] (Computation and Language). Submitted 25 Nov 2025 (v1), last revised 26 Nov 2025 (v2). DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2511.19957. CC BY 4.0. No peer-reviewed venue as of mid-2026; preprint only.
authors_affiliation: Tianyi Chen* (corresponding, Tianyi.Chen@microsoft.com) and Michael Solodko* [equal contribution]; Sen Wang, Jongwoo Ko, Junheng Hao, Colby Banbury, Sara Abdali, Saeed Amizadeh, Qing Xiao, Yinheng Li, Tianyu Ding, Kamran Ghasedi Dizaji, Suzhen Zheng, Hao Fan, Justin Wagle, Pashmina Cameron, Kazuhito Koishida. Single affiliation: Microsoft.
task_domain: tool-use / decision-making for computer-using agents (CUAs): application-level tool selection, i.e., choosing which desktop application to use to accomplish a natural-language user task BEFORE invoking fine-grained tools/APIs within that application. A higher-level inter-application reasoning problem distinct from intra-application API selection.
problem_setting: Offline, single-step, single-agent evaluation benchmark (not an interactive multi-turn execution loop). The task is formalized as a graph-structured prediction f: U -> G(T) mapping a natural-language user intent U to a directed graph over a candidate application set T={t_1,...,t_n} whose vertices are applications and whose edges encode temporal/logical/data dependencies (singleton, sequential chain, or parallel/branched). In this version the authors deliberately restrict the FOCUS AND SCOPE to the singleton-application setting: each task is solved by a single application or a few interchangeable alternatives; sequential/parallel multi-application scenarios are explicitly left to future versions. Supervision: each user task is paired with a ground-truth set of valid applications (multi-label via an application-equivalence mapping). Evaluation is one-shot prediction of an application name from a fixed candidate list of 100 apps, under deterministic decoding (temperature=0). Five protocols are compared: LLM-free Random Selector and Rule-based Heuristic, and LLM-driven Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Retrieval-Augmented Selection (RAS). No tool execution / GUI grounding is performed; the benchmark isolates inter-application reasoning from execution fidelity.
what_is_retrieved: tools (applications): in the Retrieval-Augmented Selection (RAS) protocol the model is provided with structured application descriptions (core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios) for each candidate application, retrieved from an external knowledge base; these serve as lightweight factual grounding about the available tools. In the Few-Shot protocol, annotated task->application demonstration examples are provided instead (not framed as retrieval).
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: RAS retrieves from a fixed external knowledge base of application descriptions (capability/functionality/usage profiles for the 100 desktop applications). It is NOT a growing/episodic agent-written memory; the store is predefined and frozen during evaluation.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Variable-size / membership-based correctness over a multi-valid label set rather than a fixed top-k ranking: because many tasks admit multiple valid applications (grouped via an application-equivalence mapping), a prediction is counted correct if it belongs to the annotated set of valid applications. In the studied singleton setting the model outputs a single application name (effectively top-1) judged against the valid set; the broader graph formulation targets recovery of the complete set/structure of needed applications, but multi-application completeness is left to future versions.
retrieval_unit: tool-API (here at the application granularity): one application's structured description record (name + core capabilities + functionalities + typical usage scenarios) is the retrievable unit in RAS. For Few-Shot, the unit is a single task->application demonstration example.
index_source: Static corpus built offline: an external knowledge base of structured per-application capability/usage descriptions for the 100 curated desktop applications, plus (separately) the benchmark's own atomic-task database (~3,000 atomic tasks) and >100k generated user task-application pairs used as data, not as a test-time-growing retrievable store. The retrievable RAS index is predefined and not induced online from agent trajectories.
index_structure_topology: Flat per-application description list in the RAS prompt (an 'Application tool list' of name: capabilities pairs). The underlying application taxonomy is hierarchical (12 high-level categories -> applications) and the problem is framed as a directed dependency GRAPH over applications, but the RAS retrievable store itself is presented as a flat enumerated list of application descriptions rather than a graph/cluster index. [uncertain] whether an embedding vector index is used to select which descriptions to include vs. injecting the whole candidate list.
retriever_type: [uncertain]: the paper describes RAS as providing application descriptions 'retrieved from an external knowledge base' but does not specify the retriever implementation (e.g., dense embedding vs. lookup vs. injecting all candidate descriptions). The example shows the full application tool list provided to the model, suggesting a lookup/enumeration of candidate-application descriptions rather than a learned ranker. The separate Rule-based Heuristic baseline uses semantic lexicon matching (sum/cell/spreadsheet -> Excel), approximating a deterministic keyword retrieval system.
retriever_learning_signal: none (off-the-shelf / no trained retriever): RAS grounding is fixed structured descriptions from a knowledge base; there is no contrastive, LM-feedback, preference, or RL training of a retriever. The Rule-based Heuristic likewise uses fixed predefined application-specific lexicons. No learned retrieval policy is trained.
query_construction: Raw user task description: the natural-language user intent (e.g., 'I want to know the stock price of Microsoft') is used directly as the query, paired in the prompt with the retrieved application descriptions. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent-extraction stage is described for RAS.
query_granularity: task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single retrieval/grounding step per user task; the model makes one application-selection decision for the whole task. No step-level or two-level retrieval (the studied scope is singleton selection).
when_to_retrieve: one-shot: grounding (application descriptions in RAS, or demonstrations in Few-Shot) is provided once up front before the single selection decision. No iterative, uncertainty-triggered, or learned-router retrieval.
retrieval_trigger_signal: fixed schedule / protocol-determined: retrieval is not adaptively triggered; it is a fixed property of the RAS evaluation protocol (always provide the external application descriptions for every task). There is no token-confidence, attention, learned-complexity, reflection-token, or agent-initiated retrieval signal.
reranking: None: no reranking stage (no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking) is described; the application descriptions are injected as context and the LLM directly selects.
retrieved_context_refinement: None / minimal: the retrieved application descriptions are described as 'lightweight factual grounding' injected directly into the prompt as an application tool list. No decompose-recompose, distillation, distractor filtering, or compression of the retrieved descriptions is reported.
how_retrieved_used: prompt augmentation: the retrieved structured application descriptions (RAS) or annotated demonstration examples (Few-Shot) are concatenated into the LLM prompt alongside the user task to inform a single application-selection decision. There is no skill reuse, case adaptation, training signal, or latent-token injection; retrieval is purely in-context grounding tested against a frozen LLM.
planning_integration: retrieve-then-select (one-shot exemplars/grounding at decision time): in the studied singleton scope there is no multi-step plan; RAS/Few-Shot context is provided once and the model directly predicts the application. The broader graph formulation envisions selecting a structured set/sequence of applications (plan-like), but multi-application planning is left to future work; no MCTS/tree search or per-step interleaving is used.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: per-answer: a single retrieval/grounding step feeds a single application-selection answer per task; retrieval is not interleaved per-CoT-step, per-token, or per-tool-call.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured note / capability profile injected as free text: for RAS, an 'Application tool list' where each application is paired with a concise capability/functionality/usage description (e.g., 'Excel: Supports tabular editing, formulas, data visualization'). For Few-Shot, raw task->application mapping exemplars (e.g., 'Create a bar chart from a table -> Excel'). Not executable programs, full trajectories, or latent tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Distilled capability description (RAS): a high-level summary of each application's core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios, i.e., a structured factual profile rather than a raw trajectory, procedural skill, or reusable workflow. Few-Shot units are single demonstrations (task->app hints).
noise_robustness_mechanism: None explicit: no retriever-aware training, relevance evaluator, self-reflection, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT is built in. The paper instead empirically observes that RAS helps mid-scale/open models (+3-5%) but yields non-monotonic / sometimes negative effects for very small models (e.g., gemma-3-270m drops to chance under RAS), noting retrieval helps only when the model can meaningfully integrate the structured descriptions into its reasoning.
memory_type: none: there is no episodic, skill-library, workflow, procedural, graph, or latent memory. The external application-description knowledge base is a static reference corpus, not an agent-written memory.
write_back: false: the system does not write new experiences/cases/skills into a retrievable memory. The >100k user tasks and atomic-task database are generated offline as benchmark data, not test-time write-back.
online_growth: false: the retrievable application-description store (and the benchmark task set) is fixed during evaluation; it does not grow from agent outputs at test time.
write_back_trigger: never: no automatic memory write-back exists. Tasks and atomic-task/composition databases are created offline via a GPT-5-plus-human-annotation generation pipeline, not triggered by inference-time success/failure or reflection.
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none: failed experiences are not stored or retrieved. The paper performs offline error analysis (category-level confusion matrices, intra- vs cross-category error decomposition, per-application F1) to characterize failure modes, but these are diagnostic analyses, not persisted negative cases used for retrieval or learning.
memory_evolution_update: N/A: there is no model-written memory to mutate. The static application knowledge base and benchmark data are updated only by the offline curation pipeline (GPT-5 drafting + human refinement), not via append/dedup/refine of agent memory.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: application selection is performed by a frozen LLM in-context (or by fixed Random/Rule-based baselines); RAS grounding and the retriever are fixed/non-learned. There is no RL- or value-learned retrieval/selection policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: single-model evaluation against a shared static knowledge base; no cross-agent or cross-framework memory/experience sharing. Multiple LLMs are evaluated independently and confusion patterns are aggregated across models only for diagnostic analysis.
benchmarks: AppSelectBench (introduced by this paper): 100 widely used desktop applications across 12 high-level categories; an atomic-task database of ~3,000 atomic tasks; >100,000 (one hundred thousand+) realistic user task-application pairs, averaging ~1,000 high-quality tasks per application; an application-equivalence mapping grouping functionally overlapping tools. Evaluation covers all 12 categories under 5 protocols (Random, Rule-based Heuristic, Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, RAS).
benchmark_family: tool (application/tool-selection benchmark) for computer-using agents (CUAs). Positioned alongside API-level tool benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolBench/ToolLLM, Gorilla/APIBench, ToolAlpaca, ToolQA, MetaTool, StableToolBench) and CUA environments (OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena, WinSpot), but it uniquely targets the application-selection layer rather than API selection or end-to-end GUI execution.
baselines: LLM-free baselines: Random Selector and Rule-based Heuristic (semantic lexicon matching). LLM-driven models (closed-source): GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini. Open-source: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3-8B, Phi-4, gemma-3-270m, gemma-3-4b-pt. Each evaluated under Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and RAS.
key_metrics: (1) Tool selection accuracy = proportion of user tasks whose predicted application lies within the annotated set of valid solutions (membership-based, multi-valid; not exact-match). (2) Confusion analysis: row-normalized category-level confusion matrices; decomposition of misclassifications into intra-category substitution rate (pi_intra) vs cross-category boundary errors (pi_cross). (3) Per-application precision/recall/F1. Data-quality metrics: 5-point Likert grammatical naturalness, semantic realism, and ground-truth correctness from human evaluation.
headline_result: On AppSelectBench (overall accuracy averaged across zero-shot/few-shot/RAS), GPT-5 is best at 63.3%, followed by GPT-4o-mini at 60.3%; the Random Selector lower bound is ~1.6% and the Rule-based Heuristic reaches ~56%. Even the strongest model (GPT-5) leaves a large gap to perfect, showing that LLMs still struggle to make consistent application choices. Best single cell: GPT-5 RAS = 0.644 overall.
ablations: (1) Protocol/supervision ablation (the core study): Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot vs RAS per model. Few-shot yields consistent but moderate gains (~+2%); RAS delivers the largest improvements for mid-scale/open models (+3-5%, e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B 53.0->55.0->57.4), while high-capacity models (GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini) gain only ~1-2% since semantics are already internalized; very small models (gemma-3-270m) are unstable and degrade under RAS (0.024 zero-shot/RAS vs 0.244 few-shot), showing retrieval helps only when the model can integrate structured descriptions. (2) Error-type decomposition: pi_intra=0.234 vs pi_cross=0.766, i.e., cross-category boundary errors dominate, motivating hierarchical category-then-application selection. (3) Category-difficulty analysis: easiest Streaming & Social Video (0.623), Windows Core Apps & System Utilities (0.581); hardest Gaming & Game Utilities (0.331), Music & Media Players (0.354) due to near-substitutable tools; rankings stable across models. (4) Per-application F1: distinctive apps high (Microsoft Word F1=0.96) vs broad/overlapping apps low (Notepad F1=0.50). (5) Data-quality study: human Likert grammatical 4.7, semantic realism 4.6, ground-truth correctness 99.8% on a 10% (~100/app) sample, 3 annotators each.
evaluation_decoupling: No / not applicable in the standard sense: AppSelectBench's end-to-end task metric IS the retrieval/selection accuracy (selecting the correct application). Intrinsic retrieval metrics like Recall@k/nDCG over the RAS knowledge base are not reported separately; instead application-selection accuracy, per-application precision/recall/F1, and confusion matrices serve as the selection-quality metrics. There is no downstream execution metric to decouple from (execution is intentionally out of scope).
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both outcome and process diagnostics: outcome is application-selection accuracy; process/diagnostic depth is provided via category-level confusion matrices, intra- vs cross-category error decomposition, per-category accuracy, and per-application F1, which localize WHERE inter-application reasoning fails (e.g., Edge<->Chrome, YouTube<->Netflix confusions; Cloud Storage leaking into Windows Core).
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Not a focus: no retrieval-call counts, API cost, latency, token-savings, or rollout numbers are reported. The motivation frames application selection as improving downstream context efficiency (resolving the app first lets a CUA focus on relevant APIs and ignore irrelevant tools), but no quantitative cost/efficiency measurements are given. Inference uses deterministic decoding (temperature=0).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed protocol-determined context: Zero-Shot provides only the task; Few-Shot adds a small fixed number of demonstration examples; RAS injects an 'Application tool list' of per-application capability descriptions (a fixed candidate set of 100 applications is enumerated in the evaluation system prompt). The model outputs a single application name (top-1) per task. No token-budget figures or adaptive-k selection are reported; [uncertain] exact number of few-shot exemplars and whether all 100 descriptions are injected in RAS.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Size: 100 desktop applications across 12 categories; ~3,000 atomic tasks; >100,000 user task-application pairs (~1,000 per application). Construction: a 4-stage LLM-synthesized + human-refined pipeline -- (1) atomic-task database curated by GPT-5 drafting then human annotation; (2) a composition engine samples/composes atomic tasks into intra- and inter-application workflows (also GPT-5-curated, human-refined); (3) an argument generator instantiates realistic values via rule-based templates, probabilistic sampling, and generative models; (4) an instruction narrator aggregates step instructions, applies step-wise drop-out, then LLM rephrasing to produce fluent natural-language user tasks. An application-equivalence mapping handles multi-valid ground truth. Answer verifiability: high (membership against curated valid-application sets; human-validated 99.8% ground-truth correctness on a 10% sample). Difficulty signal: best system GPT-5 reaches only ~63.3% overall accuracy, indicating substantial headroom and genuine inter-application ambiguity.
builds_on: API-level tool-selection benchmarks it extends/contextualizes: API-Bank (Li et al., 2023), ToolBench (Xu et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2023), Gorilla/APIBench (Patil et al., 2024), ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023), ToolQA (Zhuang et al., 2023), MetaTool (Huang et al., 2023), StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024). Tool-augmented LLM foundations: Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023), ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), PAL (Gao et al., 2023), MINT (Wang et al., 2024). CUA environments it complements: OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024), Windows Agent Arena (Bonatti et al., 2024), WinSpot (Hui et al., 2025), OpenCUA, UI-TARS-2, UltraCUA, Phi-Ground. Models used: GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5/Qwen3, Llama-3, Phi-4, Gemma-3.
contrasts_with: Explicitly contrasts API-LEVEL selection (intra-tool function calls within a pre-selected application, e.g., SUM(range) in Excel; input = user task + pre-selected app; output = sequence of API calls; core challenge = argument binding/sequencing) against its own APPLICATION-LEVEL selection (inter-application choice, e.g., Excel vs Calculator; input = user task only; output = set of suitable applications; core challenge = high-level intent matching) per Table 1. Also contrasts with CUA benchmarks (OSWorld, Windows Agent Arena) that preload the relevant application and thus bypass the application-selection step that AppSelectBench isolates.
lineage: Group E (tool-use): a 2025 benchmark introducing the application-selection layer for computer-using agents, situated above API-level tool-retrieval/selection benchmarks (API-Bank, Gorilla, ToolBench/ToolLLM, ToolRet) and orthogonal to end-to-end CUA execution benchmarks (OSWorld, WAA). Its retrieval-augmented (RAS) protocol connects to the tool-retrieval line, but its contribution is benchmark + evaluation protocols for inter-application reasoning rather than a new retrieval method.
code_url: https://github.com/microsoft/appselectbench [uncertain: linked from the official project page https://microsoft.github.io/appselectbench/ but returns HTTP 404 / not resolvable as of mid-2026, i.e., not yet public]. Project/source page: https://microsoft.github.io/appselectbench/ (live).
maintained_repo_url: https://microsoft.github.io/appselectbench/ (official Microsoft project homepage with abstract, app-coverage tables, pipeline figures, and results; links to the intended GitHub repo https://github.com/microsoft/appselectbench which is not yet publicly resolvable). No live leaderboard maintained.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: partial (RAS retrieves static application descriptions; Few-Shot retrieves demonstration exemplars), Reuse: no (no prior solved case is reused/adapted), Revise: no, Retain: no]. Not a case-based-reasoning system; it grounds selection in tool descriptions/demonstrations, not in prior solved problem-solution cases.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is an application-selection benchmark with retrieval-augmented and few-shot grounding protocols.
tool_document_engineering: Application descriptions for the RAS knowledge base are engineered into concise structured capability profiles capturing each app's core capabilities, functionalities, and typical usage scenarios (e.g., 'Excel: Supports tabular editing, formulas, data visualization'). No synthetic-query augmentation, expanded summaries, weighted-field embeddings, or instruction-tuned tool embeddings are reported; the Rule-based Heuristic separately uses hand-built application-specific lexicons.
index_content_separation: Partial / lightweight grounding by design: RAS injects 'lightweight factual grounding' (compact capability descriptions) rather than heavy full documentation, and the application identity is decoupled from any (out-of-scope) underlying APIs/execution. But there is no explicit progressive-disclosure index-then-content mechanism; the descriptions are provided directly in-context.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Static, no live tool protocol: the application set (100 apps) and their RAS descriptions are predefined and frozen; there is no live RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling synchronization or CRUD auto-sync. The benchmark evaluates selection in the abstract, decoupled from any live tool-execution protocol.
tool_dependency_awareness: Modeled in the formulation but not in the evaluated scope: the problem is defined as a directed graph whose edges encode temporal/logical/data dependencies between applications (singleton, sequential chain e.g. Browser->PowerPoint, parallel/branched), and the generation pipeline composes inter-application workflows (e.g., ExcelExportChart->PowerPointInsertTable). However, the evaluated FOCUS is the singleton-application setting, so inter-application dependency prediction is largely left to future versions; no dependency-aware retrieval/reranking is used.
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR): the closest analogue is that the model reads retrieved application descriptions (RAS) or task->app demonstrations (Few-Shot) and uses them as in-context grounding to select an application; no prior solved case is adapted or revised.
